lpc.story.numidicus.heart: Cyprian added Numidicus to the presbyters of Carthage. Numidicus had urged others to martyrdom, watched his wife burn, and been left for dead. He stayed behind against his will. We kept the story because it calls a martyr's death a completion, not a loss, and honours a man who did not want to survive.

lpc.story.numidicus.telling_short: Cyprian wrote that he was adding Numidicus to our presbyters. "By his urging he sent a great number of martyrs ahead of himself, killed by stones and by fire." Cyprian wrote that his wife was burned with them, then corrected himself. "I should rather say she was preserved." We called her death a completion, not a loss. Numidicus was half burned, buried under stones and left for dead. His daughter searched for his body. He was found half dead and revived. He stayed behind against his will. The Lord, Cyprian said, meant to add him to our clergy.
lpc.story.numidicus.telling_medium:
Cyprian wrote to us that he was adding Numidicus to the presbyters of Carthage.

"By his urging he sent a great number of martyrs ahead of himself, killed by stones and by fire." His own wife died with them. "With joy he watched his wife, who stayed at his side, burned with the others," Cyprian wrote, and then corrected himself. "I should rather say she was preserved." For us, a martyr's death was a completion, not a loss.

"He himself was half burned, buried under stones and left for dead." His daughter came looking for her father's body "with the anxious care of love." He was found half dead, pulled out and revived.

"Against his will, he stayed behind the companions he himself had sent ahead." Cyprian saw a reason why he survived. The Lord meant to add Numidicus to our clergy.

lpc.story.election-of-cyprian.heart: Our deacon Pontius says God's judgment and the people's favour made Cyprian bishop, though he was newly baptized. We kept it because the people's favour was how God's judgment became visible to us.

lpc.story.election-of-cyprian.telling_short: Our deacon Pontius wrote the life of Cyprian after his bishop had been put to death. "By the judgment of God and the favour of the people, he was chosen for the sacred office and the rank of bishop. He was still newly baptized and, as people thought, a beginner." For Pontius, the people's favour was how God's judgment became visible to us. Years later, answering rivals, Cyprian called it our suffrage, joined to God's judgment.
lpc.story.election-of-cyprian.telling_medium:
Our deacon Pontius wrote the life of Cyprian after his bishop had been put to death. He said one fact was proof enough of Cyprian's good works.

"By the judgment of God and the favour of the people, he was chosen for the sacred office and the rank of bishop. He was still newly baptized and, as people thought, a beginner."

Cyprian did not reach for the office. When the whole people leapt forward in love for him, Pontius says, he humbly stepped back. He gave way to older men and thought himself unworthy. A crowd of the brothers besieged the doors of his house.

For Pontius, the people's favour was how God's judgment became visible to us.

Years later, rivals who had never accepted him renewed their attack. Cyprian wrote to us that they still carried "that old venom against my office as bishop, which means against your suffrage and against God's judgment."
